questions.q: What can a man who finds some indecent thing in his wife do to divorce her?
questions.a: If a man has found some indecent thing in his wife, he can write her a letter of divorce, give the paper to her, and send her out of his house where she can go and become another man’s wife.

questions.q: What does Yahweh not allow if the second husband writes her a letter of divorce and sends her out of the house or if he dies?
questions.a: Yahweh does not allow for the first husband who sent her away to take her again to be his wife.

questions.q: What are the benefits for a man who has taken a new wife?
questions.a: He does not have to go to war or be commanded to go on forced duty, but he can stay home for one year to make his new wife happy.

questions.q: Why were they not allowed to take a mill or an upper millstone as a pledge from another?
questions.a: They were not to take a millstone as a pledge because it would be taking a man’s livelihood away from him.

questions.q: What are the circumstances when a man would be declared a thief and must die?
questions.a: A man would be declared a thief who must die if he kidnaps a fellow Israelite and treats him as a slave or sells him.

questions.q: What word of caution from Yahweh about leprosy did Moses pass on to the people of Israel?
questions.a: Moses told them to carefully observe and follow every instruction which Yahweh gave to the priests regarding any plague of leprosy.

questions.q: What restrictions were given when collecting a pledge on a loan made to a neighbor?
questions.a: They were not to go into the house to get the pledge, but stand outside and wait for the man who received the loan to bring out the pledge.

questions.q: What must happen if a man gives his cloak as a pledge because he is a poor man?
questions.a: If the poor man gives his cloak as a pledge for a loan, the one who gives him the loan must not keep the cloak overnight, but must take it back to him by the time the sun goes down so he may sleep in his cloak.

questions.q: What must they do for a hired servant who is poor and needy?
questions.a: They must give him his wages every day because he is poor and is counting on it.

questions.q: How did Yahweh make it clear that everyone was responsible for their own sins?
questions.a: Yahweh told the people of Israel that the parents must not be put to death for the sins of their children and the children must not be put to death for the sins of their parents.

questions.q: Why were the people of Israel reminded about their time of slavery in Egypt and how Yahweh rescued them from there?
questions.a: They were reminded so that they would follow Yahweh’s commands about how to treat foreigners, orphans, and widows.

questions.q: What were the people of Israel commanded to do when they harvested their field or shook their olive tree?
questions.a: When they harvested their crops, they were not to go back for a forgotten sheaf in the field or to beat their olive tree a second time to get more olives, but to leave them for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.

commentary.text: Of new-married persons, Of man-stealers, Of pledges.

Verses 1–4 Where the providence of God, or his own wrong choice in marriage, has allotted to a Christian a trial instead of a help meet; he will from his heart prefer bearing the cross, to such relief as tends to sin, confusion, and misery. Divine grace will sanctify this cross, support under it, and teach so to behave, as will gradually render it more tolerable.

It is of great consequence that love be kept up between husband and wife; that they carefully avoid every thing which might make them strange one to another. Man-stealing was a capital crime, which could not be settled, as other thefts, by restitution. The laws concerning leprosy must be carefully observed. Thus all who feel their consciences under guilt and wrath, must not cover it, or endeavour to shake off their convictions; but by repentance, and prayer, and humble confession, take the way to peace and pardon. Some orders are given about pledges for money lent. This teaches us to consult the comfort and subsistence of others, as much as our own advantage. Let the poor debtor sleep in his own raiment, and praise God for thy kindness to him. Poor debtors ought to feel more than commonly they do, the goodness of creditors who do not take all the advantage of the law against them, nor should this ever be looked upon as weakness.

It is not hard to prove that purity, piety, justice, mercy, fair conduct, kindness to the poor and destitute, consideration for them, and generosity of spirit, are pleasing to God, and becoming in his redeemed people. The difficulty is to attend to them in our daily walk and conversation.
